title: Operations Management Adventure 3: Supply Chain & Location
welcome_lead: Today you'll trace a supply chain, weigh R&D and choose a location.
meta_desc: Business Management Ops: supply chain management, R&D, and location decisions.
final_note: You analysed supply chains, R&D investment and key location factors.

concepts.def: Sequence from raw material to consumer

walkthroughs.body_html:
A supply chain links every step from raw material to consumer.

Effective SCM cuts costs (bulk, JIT), reduces lead times and builds resilience.

Risks include single sourcing, geopolitical disruption (COVID-19, Suez 2021) and reputational issues (sweatshops, conflict minerals).

Outsourcing hands a function to another firm; offshoring moves it abroad.

Benefits: cost savings, focus on core competence, 24-hour operations.

Costs: loss of control, quality risks, hidden coordination cost, reputational risk if labour standards are poor.

Reshoring has grown post-2020 as firms prioritise resilience.

Quantitative: land cost, labour cost, transport, taxes.

Qualitative: proximity to customers, supplier clusters, skills, regulation, government incentives, ethical concerns.

Service firms (banks) follow markets; heavy manufacturers (steel) follow raw materials.

Why can a profitable business still fail?
options: Because cash flow and profit are different — a business may be profitable on paper but run out of cash to pay bills, especially if customers owe money or stock ties up funds.
Laissez-faire leadership is illegal under employment law.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.

mcqs.q: What is a brand in marketing?
options: A combination of name, design, symbols and associations that distinguishes a product and creates customer perception and loyalty — more than just a logo.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
A brand is just the logo on a product.
A brand is the company that makes a product.

mcqs.q: When can a laissez-faire leadership style be effective?
options: Laissez-faire leadership means the leader doesn't care about the business.
Profitable businesses fail only when employees steal.
When employees are highly skilled, self-motivated and need autonomy — common in creative or expert teams. It can fail with inexperienced staff or in crises requiring direction.
Laissez-faire leadership is illegal under employment law.
